title: The doctor who seemed to die
hookLine: teaching shaped to the listener, like a doctor fitting the medicine to the patient
carry: skillful means: the teaching fitted to the listener

cards: A doctor comes home from a journey and finds that his sons, while he was away, got into his medicines and swallowed poison. Some are clear-headed enough to take the cure he mixes.
Others are so far gone that they refuse it; to them it smells wrong. So the doctor does something strange. He leaves again, and sends a messenger home to say their father has died.
The shock clears their heads. Grieving, they take the medicine he left behind, and recover. Then he comes home.
That story is from the Lotus Sutra.

teach.b: First, the idea. Upaya means a means, a method. Skillful means is teaching shaped to whoever is listening.

A good doctor doesn't hand every patient the same pill. In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha is that kind of doctor: different teachings fitted to different people, at different moments, with one aim. Second, the question.

teach.h: THE BURNING HOUSE: WAS IT A LIE?
teach.b: This block opened with another of the sutra's parables: the father who lures his children out of a burning house with the promise of carts, then gives each one a great cart.
Right after, the Buddha asks his disciple Shariputra: did that father lie? No, Shariputra says.
He saved his children's lives. Even if he had given them nothing at all, it would not have been a falsehood. Third, the doctor's meaning.

teach.h: THE DOCTOR WHO SEEMS TO DIE.
teach.b: The sutra asks the same of the doctor who sent word of his own death, and gives the same answer. Then the Buddha says he is like that doctor.
If people could always see him, they'd grow careless and stop reaching for the medicine. So he appears to pass away, and the missing makes them reach. Fourth, the limit, and an older echo.
Some readers point to a limit inside the stories: the trick serves the children, never the father. And the Pali texts make the point their own way.
The Buddha compares his teaching to a raft: you build it to cross a river, and once you're across, you don't carry it on your head. A teaching is a tool, made for a need.

how: Mahayana teachers speak of skillful means when they explain why the Buddha taught different things to different people, and the parables of the burning house and the physician are told in East Asian temples and study groups.

o: teaching shaped to whoever is listening, like fitted medicine
a clever trick that tests whether students are paying attention
a rule that the very same words be taught to everyone

p: sends word that he has died
says the father told no lie

s: skillful means makes any trick acceptable
in each parable the trick serves the children's good, never the teller's.
in the Lotus Sutra, Shariputra says the father in the burning house told no lie
he saved his children's lives, so it was no falsehood.
the idea of a teaching as a tool appears only in Mahayana texts
the Pali texts compare the teaching to a raft, for crossing, not for carrying.

games.q: you're the doctor. your sons have swallowed poison, and some refuse the cure because it smells wrong to them. what do you do, in the Lotus Sutra?
o: go away and send word that you have died
throw the medicine out and wait
games.why: the shock clears their heads, and they take the medicine he left. the sutra asks whether he lied, and answers no.

practice: Think of something you know well, a recipe, a game, a hard lesson life taught you, and picture explaining it to a small child, to a tired friend at the end of a long day, and to someone who doesn't quite trust you.
Notice how the words change: shorter here, gentler there, a story for the child. The thing itself stays the same; only the doorway changes.

wordCard.voice: Upaya. Skillful means: teaching shaped to the one who is listening, the way a doctor fits the medicine to the patient. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: a means, a method; in the Mahayana, the skill of fitting the teaching to the listener.

carryVoice: Your line: skillful means: the teaching fitted to the listener, the way a doctor fits the medicine to the one who takes it. Until tomorrow.
